name: Suction cup / cupping on cheeks
lead: Cupping on the cheeks is the use of small suction cups on the face, borrowed from the wider practice of cupping therapy, with the aim of giving the cheek area a fuller, livelier and more contoured look. A cup is applied to the skin and a partial vacuum draws the tissue gently upward into it; people who try it on the face do so for a temporary flush of color and a lifted appearance in the cheeks and lower face.[1]

In looksmaxxing and skincare circles the technique is discussed as a low-cost, at-home way to work on facial appearance. Proponents describe the suction as bringing blood to the surface of the skin, which they associate with a healthier-looking complexion and a lifted look. Cupping on the body has been used in many traditions, from Chinese and Middle Eastern medicine to ancient Greece, and the face version is an adaptation of it, typically with small, softer cups and lighter suction than those used on the back.[1]

Cupping in general leaves circular marks where small capillaries beneath the skin respond to the suction. A 2020 eye-tracking study of cupping marks found that people notice and attend to these marks, which is one reason facial cupping is often described as done with light suction and short sessions.[2] No published trials have tested cheek cupping for cosmetic results.

chain: Suction cup draws cheek skin into the cup
Temporary flush and lift in the area
angle.text: People use small suction cups on the cheeks hoping for a temporary lift, a flush of color and a more contoured look. The effect described by users is short-lived and tied to the suction session itself.

card.summary: Small suction cups applied to the cheeks to draw up the skin for a temporary flushed, lifted look.
card.note: Suction can leave temporary round marks on the skin.

quick.overview:
Facial cupping uses small suction cups on the cheeks. Users hope it gives a fuller, more lifted and more colorful cheek area, and it is usually done in short sessions with light suction.

It is an offshoot of traditional body cupping, adapted for the face. Results people describe are temporary, and no published trials have tested it for cheek shaping.
quick.mechanism: A cup creates a partial vacuum that pulls skin and underlying tissue upward into it. This briefly brings blood to the surface, which proponents link to a flushed, lifted look.
quick.risks: Suction can break tiny capillaries and leave circular marks or bruises, and strong suction on thin facial skin is where most reported marks come from. Cupping is generally regarded as suitable for most people when done by trained practitioners, but conditions such as eczema or psoriasis can be aggravated.

paras: Cups used on the face are typically small silicone or plastic cups that are squeezed or pumped to create suction, in contrast to the larger glass or bamboo cups used on the back. Cupping therapy more broadly includes dry cupping (suction only), fire cupping, and wet cupping, and cups may be left in place or glided over oiled skin as a cup massage.[1]

Cupping sessions in traditional settings usually last between five and fifteen minutes per placement, and suction strength is classed as light, medium or strong.[1] Facial applications are generally described at the light end of that range.

Practitioners distinguish several ways of using a cup on the skin. In stationary cupping the cup stays in one spot for a short period; in gliding or cup massage the cup is moved over oiled skin; in flash cupping it is applied and released repeatedly. Wikipedia describes cup massage as being used on almost any area of the body, from the back and limbs to the face, with sessions of roughly ten to twenty minutes on the body, accompanied by warmth and possibly some discomfort.[1] Facial versions use smaller, softer cups at the lighter end of the suction range.[1]

Wikipedia describes the origin of cupping as unclear. It records Hippocrates (about 460 to 370 BC) using cupping for internal disease, Roman surgeons using it for bloodletting, and Islamic medicine recommending and elaborating wet cupping (hijama), which remains popular in many Muslim-majority regions.[1] The earliest recorded Chinese use is attributed to the Taoist alchemist Ge Hong (281 to 341 AD), and Chinese hospitals have used it as a traditional Chinese medicine modality since the 1950s.[1] In Finland, wet cupping with horn cups has been practised in saunas since the 15th century.[1]

Classification schemes in the literature sort cupping by technique (dry, wet, massage, flash), suction strength (light, medium, strong) and method (fire, manual, electrical), and later schemes add categories by treated area, including facial.[1]

Facial cupping is discussed as a do-it-yourself approach to cheek definition and skin glow, alongside other manual face techniques such as massage and gua sha. Users describe moving the cup across the cheek or holding it briefly in place. Because the marks cupping can leave are visible, users commonly describe keeping suction light on the face.[2]

Facial gua sha, a related scraping practice, became popular with beauty influencers on social media around 2021 to 2022, for claimed lymphatic drainage and skin freshening; cupping on the face is often presented in the same circles.[3]

The look people seek is temporary: a flushed, plumped cheek immediately after a session and the sense of a lifted midface. Users position it with other soft-tissue routines, such as facial massage, gua sha and skincare, rather than as a structural change to bone or fat, and commonly keep sessions short so that no marks are left on a visible area.[2][3]

Proponents of cupping in traditional Chinese medicine say suction dispels stagnation of blood and lymph and improves the flow of qi, often when cups are placed on acupuncture points.[1] Facial cupping users describe the same idea in cosmetic terms: more blood to the surface, a brighter complexion and a gentle lift. Wikipedia's article notes that cup massage can be done on almost any area of the body, including the face, and cites a news article about facial vacuum treatments for glowing skin, without evaluating evidence for facial use.[1]

Wikipedia notes that journalist James Hamblin pointed out that a cupping bruise is a pooled blood clot rather than flowing blood, and that this is raised against the improved-circulation explanation; Wikipedia presents both the traditional explanations and this critique without resolving them.[1]

On the body, cups cause breaks in small capillaries in the upper dermis, producing petechiae and purpura, seen as dark red or purple discs; wet cupping can leave linear streaks and fire cupping can leave darker circles.[1] The marks typically fade over days to a couple of weeks. This matters for the face because the marks are conspicuous: a 2020 eye-tracking study found that viewers' attention is drawn to cupping marks, which is one reason people who try cheek cupping describe using gentle suction and brief contact.[2]

No published trial has tested cupping the cheeks for contour, skin colour or any cosmetic outcome. The wider cupping literature is mostly about musculoskeletal pain. Wikipedia lists a series of reviews: the American Cancer Society (2009) said available evidence did not support health-benefit claims; a 2011 review by Lee, Kim and Ernst described effectiveness as poorly documented for most conditions; a 2015 Cochrane review found no evidence supporting cupping for acne; and a 2019 review found low to moderate evidence for reduced musculoskeletal pain that might be indistinguishable from placebo.[1]

Proponents counter that cupping has a long history in several medical traditions and that the visible effects of suction, such as flush and tissue lift, are observable in the moment, which is what cosmetic users are after.[1]

Cupping reached a mass audience at the 2016 Rio Olympics, when swimmer Michael Phelps and other athletes appeared with circular marks, prompting coverage of both the practice and critics' objections.[1] Wikipedia cites a Times of India article describing facial vacuum treatments for glowing skin as an example of cosmetic cupping reaching beauty media.[1] Facial gua sha, a related practice, surged on TikTok in 2021 to 2022 through beauty influencers promoting lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation.[3]

Gua sha is a Chinese practice of scraping oiled skin with a smooth tool such as jade, ceramic or horn; Wikipedia traces its formal use to the Ming dynasty (1368 to 1644) and describes lighter pressure on the face and the redness or bruising (sha) it commonly produces.[3] Related manual face routines include facial massage, rollers and face yoga. Fire and wet cupping are separate traditional forms that carry greater risks than light dry suction.[1]

Suction breaks small capillaries under the skin, which produces circular bruises or petechiae. Other reported risks of cupping include burns with fire cupping, skin discoloration, and flare-ups of eczema or psoriasis.[1] The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health is cited as noting persistent discoloration, scars and infections as possible side effects.[1] Research on how people react to cupping marks shows they draw visual attention, which is relevant on the face.[2]

Wikipedia lists local effects of cupping that include petechiae and purpura, scarring, burns, skin ulcers, darkened skin, and triggering of the Koebner phenomenon in people with psoriasis; it says marks have occasionally been mistaken for child abuse, and that fire cupping and wet cupping carry greater risks than light dry cupping.[1]

Wikipedia says cupping is generally considered safe for most people when performed by trained practitioners, but that it may not suit everyone, and notes that Cambodia's health ministry warned in 2016 that it could be dangerous for people with high blood pressure or heart problems.[1] Skin around the eyes is thin, which is why facial guidance emphasises light suction and avoiding that area.[1]

Cupping drew wide public attention at the 2016 Olympics when swimmer Michael Phelps appeared with circular marks on his back, reportedly using it to speed recovery; athletes including Shaquille O'Neal, Natalie Coughlin and Alex Naddour have also used it, and critics such as Brad McKay and Steven Novella have objected to its use by elite athletes.[1] Facial cupping reached beauty audiences alongside gua sha and other manual face techniques promoted on social media.[3]

No studies found on cupping the cheeks. Studies of cupping therapy on the body have examined mainly pain conditions, and a 2025 randomized trial looked at its immediate effects on pain, flexibility and temperature of the lower back.[4] Reviews describe the wider cupping literature as variable in quality.[1] Wikipedia reports that the American Cancer Society states the available evidence does not support health benefit claims, that systematic reviews describe poor research quality, that there is low to moderate evidence for pain reduction that may be indistinguishable from placebo, and that there is a lack of evidence for acne.[1]

timeline.event: Hippocrates is recorded as using cupping for internal disease.[1]
The Taoist alchemist Ge Hong provides the earliest recorded Chinese use of cupping.[1]
Gua sha is formalised in Chinese medicine during the Ming dynasty.[3]
Chinese hospitals adopt cupping as a traditional medicine modality.[1]
The American Cancer Society states the available evidence does not support health-benefit claims for cupping.[1]
Michael Phelps's cupping marks at the Rio Olympics bring the practice to wide public attention.[1]
An eye-tracking study reports that viewers' attention is drawn to cupping marks.[2]
Facial gua sha and related manual face tools spread on TikTok through beauty influencers.[3]

lore.intro: Facial cupping is discussed in beauty and appearance circles as a cheap, at-home companion to massage and gua sha, with claims centred on glow and lift.[3]

claims.claim: Cheek cupping gives an instant lifted, flushed look
claims.believers: Users describe a short-lived plump, rosy cheek after a session and treat it as a free pre-event glow routine.[3]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined cheek cupping; Wikipedia's cupping article reports no clinical evidence for cosmetic benefit.[1]

claims.claim: Suction boosts circulation and brightens skin
claims.believers: Proponents say suction draws blood to the surface, giving a healthier complexion.[1]
claims.experts: Journalist James Hamblin has noted a cupping bruise is a clotted pool of blood rather than flowing blood, as summarised by Wikipedia.[1]

claims.claim: It drains lymph and de-puffs the face
claims.believers: Beauty influencers promote gua sha and cupping for lymphatic drainage and a slimmer look.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says gua sha lacks high-quality evidence of clinical benefit.[3]

claims.claim: Used lightly, it leaves no marks
claims.believers: Users say short sessions with light suction avoid visible circles.[2]
claims.experts: Cupping commonly produces petechiae and purpura, and an eye-tracking study found viewers notice such marks.[1][2]

claims.believers: Some facial-cupping sellers and users suggest it clears skin.[1]
claims.experts: A 2015 Cochrane review found no evidence supporting cupping for acne, per Wikipedia.[1]

claims.believers: Users regard it as gentler than body cupping.[3]
claims.experts: Documented local effects of cupping include bruising, scarring, burns with fire cupping and flare-ups of eczema or psoriasis.[1]
